explanation: No clear shared feature. Strong activations land on very different tokens: structural spots in code or JSON (opening braces, '<' in XML or trees, a space before a SPARQL variable), digits inside numbers, subword fragments in OCR or foreign text, and plain function words. Mid and weak examples are ordinary function words and digits in prose.

Fires on the plural subject pronoun 'they'/'They' starting a clause, strongest after a subordinator or connective (so, because, while, as, and) and referring back to a plural noun mentioned earlier. It also fires somewhat on plural noun subjects (Prebiotics, Tickets, articles). Other subject pronouns (we, I) give moderate activation; non-subject tokens give little.

Fires mostly on the first letter or first subword of a proper place or person name, especially names starting with 'K' (Kilkenny, Kettering, Kralingse, Kensington, KTV, de Kooning), and on 'at' before a venue name. Separate strong hits also occur on argument separators in code (a comma or quote inside a function call) and on scattered content words.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a word the tokenizer has split, usually a capitalized name or technical identifier (J-av-itz, N-al-bari, P-open, P-IVOT, up-sert, L-ints, E-clipse, e.g.), and on fragments of Greek, Finnish or Norwegian words. The model must then complete the word. Weak activation on ordinary prose words.

Tends to fire early in a document, in title, heading, abstract-opening or license-boilerplate text: function words in fixed phrases ('list of conditions', '(the "License")'), suffix completions of a title term (Notostylopidae, eponymous, GRADE), and the first word after a header. The common thread is weak.

Mixed. Fires strongly on the generic or addressee pronoun 'you' in conversational advice ('depends who you ask', 'you have to pay', 'Generally you don't want'). Unrelated strong hits include Turkish and Spanish word pieces, name fragments, a math '(i', and various content words.

Fires on commas that separate items in a list or series, especially between coordinated adjectives or nouns ('personal, academic', 'DIRECT, INDIRECT', 'argc, char'). It also fires on the comma after the day in a date ('March 12, 1997'). Weaker on clause-level commas and on 'and' inside lists.

Fires on short function words (mostly 'a' and 'at', also 'be', 'per', 'my', 'is') inside idiomatic or measurement phrases that predict a specific next word: 'diameter at breast height', 'a few', 'a lot', 'worth a pound', 'per game', 'about my day', 'high at the closing bell'.

Fires on a token inside a set technical or brand compound where the next part is highly predictable: 'pop3', 'breastfeeds', 'exterior algebra', 'mammary', 'e-mail', 'ProtonMail', and especially 'under' in the license header 'Licensed under the Apache License'. Activation is moderate overall, with one peak.

No identifiable feature. It fires about equally on unrelated tokens: verbs after 'instead of', 'Below', code braces and spacing, contraction 't, chemistry subwords, relative pronouns 'which'/'where', 'a' before quantity nouns, and 'you'.

Mixed. One clear cluster is the year digits in Wikipedia biography categories and dates ('Category:1988 births', '1950 deaths'). Other strong hits are sports-career words (win, career, final season, year) and code tokens ('<' in XML, '.get', ').'). The rest are scattered content words.

Fires on the number word 'two' used as a count or determiner for a noun ('these two types', 'any two edges', 'the other two', 'Part Two'). It fires moderately on the digit '2' at the start of numbers and dates and on 'both'.

Fires on a word-initial fragment that begins a longer word, most clearly the prefix 're' in medical or biochemical terms (reductase, resection, reactivation, reductant). It also fires on the first letters of split proper names (Jaafar, Bongaigaon, Eighth, Khuzestan, COUCH).

Fires on the verb right after a plural or compound subject noun phrase, especially when agreement is wrong ('The patients is', 'questions is', 'images is', 'checkboxes has'), or on the head noun of such a phrase ('integrins and cadherins receptors', 'rental cars databases'). This marks number agreement or the end of the subject noun phrase.

Mostly fires on the first subword or second token of a rare multi-token word or name, where the model must recall the rest (Ghouta, ignite, bullosa, benchmarks, Dillashaw, albrechti, Belcastro). It also fires on content nouns or modifiers inside technical phrases. The pattern is loose.

Fires on negating prefixes 'un'/'non' (unloading, unskilled, unreported, non-functioning) and on prepositions in travel, commerce or pricing contexts ('charges for', 'travelling on leave', 'fly on a', 'tariffs on'). The two groups are only loosely linked.

Fires on content words in biomedical abstracts, especially disease, clinical and biological terms (bioterrorism, purulent, drug user, schizophrenia, duodenum, chorea, fevers, QT syndrome) and research verbs like 'confirm'/'shown'. Inside medical or scientific prose it is broadly active; elsewhere it is weak.
No coherent pattern. Strong hits include unit symbols after numbers (cd, m), digits in model names, function words (of, from, de, the), punctuation in code and paths, and scientific subwords.

Fires on a word near the start of a document or in a boilerplate or header line that predicts a fixed continuation: license text ('COPYING', ' *', 'copyright notice'), '<?xml version', 'color space', 'n-dimensional', '16mm', medical-term fragments in titles (Hyponatremia, antiarrhythmic). The cohesion is weak.

Two groups. One is the suffix that completes a word ('scar-ves', 'Cur-ves', 'cle-aves', 'activ-ator' in plasminogen activator). The other is the verb 'filed' in legal contexts (lawsuit filed, filed a complaint). A few scattered others.

Fires on the noun that ends a collective or count noun phrase, such as 'blood samples', 'bird species', 'crew members', 'staff member', and on existential 'exist(s)' in 'there exist(s)'. It also fires on some word-ending subwords (Fisherman, silverware, Indianapolis) and Japanese particles.
